chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: How Chu Berry got the credit and Joe Davis made a fortune
summary: Sixty bands recorded it before Fletcher. Horace had not copyrighted it, publisher Joe Davis bought it outright from Chu Berry and earned over $100,000, and Horace later wrote 'Chris and His Gang'.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Yes. That was recorded, of course.
Yes, by quite a few bands. Unfortunately, Fletcher's band was the last band out of about 60 recorded it.
That's what I was wondering about.
And they got the jump on Fletcher's thing, and it was original, you know, so --
Uh-huh. What kind of record sales could you expect in those days off of what would be considered a hit? How many -- how many records would you --
Oh --

Yeah, it wasn't like the millions they're talking about now. But I tell you, I remember an incident about this particular tune. I didn't have it copyrighted or anything. I just went on and did the arrangement, I was tickled to death with it. know. And, of course, Tom, I was yelling about these things young then. And we had quite a few slick guys in those days, you know, publishers and all this. They knew all the shortcuts and whatnot. So -- in fact, it got around all over Broadway about this thing, you know, and the bands began to play it. Even the band leaders, Man, as it turned out, they recorded it before Fletcher, so it must have got popular, you know.
Well, it got out that Chu Berry wrote the tune. So all this had happened before I was aware that it was happening. So there was a publishing company right there in the Roseland

which was quite convenient. building, right upstairs, (unintelligible). I'll never forget this in my life. Called Joe Davis Music Publishing Company, Incorporated. He got together with Chu Berry as the composer, wrote the tune, and I don't think Chu made any money out of it. He bought it outright from him. In those days they knew rather than take him on a commission all those things and would take (unintelligible) sort of and take a thing, chance on the thing. He bought it outright, and the guy made over $100,000.00 with the tune in a few months.
Gee, whiz.

And he got out of the business. This was another thing -- because he found out as the thing progressed that it wasn't quite the way that it went down. So I don't know if he became nervous about it, one of those things. But it was too late to get an attorney or try to sue or one of those kind of things, because I didn't have it copyrighted, one of those things. So it was just a warning to me for future things, you know.
Yeah, a lesson.

And Chu and I didn't fall out about it. We thought it was okay, you know; we went on, because I did take the riff. But I made 32 bars, while he was playing four or eight. So what I really felt that we could have done was to work together on the thing.
Right, collaborated.
And I think it would have gone farther -- and this is what transpired. So --
Do you -- did you ever have a copy of the published music? I mean did this -- what was his name, Joe Davis, did you say?
Joe Davis is the Music Publishing Company, Incorporated, right in the Roseland building.
Do you have a copy of that, or did you ever have one?
You mean a copy of --
Of the sheet music. It -- was there any sheet music made?
I think he put the stock out on this thing.
Huh. Did anybody ever write lyrics?

No. No lyrics or anything; an instrumental. So this is the way it went down. So the only thing that I got any consolation out of, when I did get together and form a band, I wrote a tune called "Chris and His Gang," which was a part of the "Christopher Columbus" thing. I tell you, a guy who really knows the story on this thing, and I'm telling him -- he'll tell you like it is too, with Roy Eldridge. So we're still friends. So (Unintelligible). Well, I won't say any more about that, because it's water under the bridge now, and I've recuperated from that.
